newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine markets shaken by Ramos' surgery.
newsitem.headline: Philippine markets shaken by Ramos' surgery.

text.p: Philippine financial markets, which were expecting a slow Christmas week, were badly shaken on Monday by news that President Fidel Ramos underwent surgery to clear a blocked artery, brokers and traders said.
Although the 75-minute operation was successfully concluded by the time markets opened for the day, the reminder of the 68-year-old Ramos' mortality led to a massive stock market sell-off, they said.

The stock market was in a tailspin for most of the session, plunging more than 2 percent at the opening but recovering marginally near the close after doctors announced that the operation was successful.
Doctors said Ramos was recovering well after they removed the arterial blockage and that he would soon be discharged.
"We hope he is out by Christmas," said Raul Fores, director of the Makati Medical Centre, where the operation was performed.
The bourse's composite index slid 40.28 points, or 1.27 percent, closing at 3,139.92 points in moderate trade. It had plunged to 3,112.56 points earlier in the day.
Also affecting the market was a heavy sell-off in index heavyweight Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co (PLDT), brokers said.

PLDT shares were battered by a U.S. Federal Communications Commission proposal to force foreign phone companies to cut rates they charge U.S. carriers for calls from the United States, which could hurt PLDT's revenues.
The Philippine peso fell to a low of 26.315 to the dollar in heavy morning trade, but stabilised after the Central Bank intervened, posting its selling rate at 26.315.
The peso closed at 26.301 last Friday.
"Investors, especially foreign investors, are very sensitive, especially on the issue of political leadership," Joselito Dalit, a researcher at Asian Bank, told Reuters.

Ramos has been instrumental in instituting a series of economic liberalisation measures in the Philippines. In his 4-1/2 years in office, he has opened up the banking, telecommunications and power-generation sectors to foreign competition.

"In markets like the Philippines where the chief executive officer is seen as a very strong and powerful leader, the market is very sensitive on news about his health," said Raul Ruiz, vice president at Sun Hung Kai Securities.

Ricardo Puig, an analyst of Peregrine Securities, added that the absence of a likely successor also exacerbated the worries. Under Philippine law, Ramos has to step down at the end of his six-year term in 1998, but no signs have yet emerged on who is likely to succeed him.
"Investors put so much premium on the president since he has handled the economy very well," Puig said.
Brokers added that Ramos's health would remain a factor in the market in coming days.
"Not until the public is convinced that he is stable will the market resume its normal course," said Harry Liu, president at the Summit Securities brokerage.
Rates for government treasury bills at the weekly auction rose across the board because of uncertainties triggered by Ramos's health, dealers said.
The bellwether 90-day T-bill rose to an average of 11.679 percent against last week's 11.509 percent while the 363-day bill soared to 12.455 percent from 12.199.
